title: the quarry Rising
premise: August Crane, a cynical senior counting down the days at Quarry High, is assigned a college essay prompt that asks: 'What would you die to protect?' The question unlocks something buried beneath the school — an old quarry tradition that literally feeds on honest answers, and which has kept the town of Granite Falls alive for a century. As her classmates' confessions vanish into the stone and the town begins to fail, August discovers she's descended from the family who made the bargain. To graduate, she must renew the covenant by sacrificing what she loves most — or break it, freeing the town from survival at the cost of everything it was built on.
about_author: Yara Iversen grew up in a fading mill town in the Pacific Northwest, where every building seemed older than its purpose. She writes young adult fiction about stubborn kids in places that refuse to change.

chapters.title: One Hundred and Sixty-Two Days
chapters.summary: August's POV. She catalogs her remaining days at Quarry High like a prison sentence, establishing her detachment, her mother's absence, and her plan to escape via college. Beat: numb resignation cracked by a flicker of curiosity when she notices the school's foundation stones are quarried, not poured.

chapters.title: The Prompt
chapters.summary: August's POV. English teacher Mr. Voss assigns the senior essay prompt — 'What would you die to protect?' — and the room goes strangely quiet. August writes a throwaway answer about nothing. That night, the words on her page rearrange themselves into a confession she never wrote. Beat: unease.

chapters.title: Granite Falls Sings
chapters.summary: August's POV. The town is unnaturally prosperous for its size; everyone credits 'the quarry.' Her grandmother warns her not to answer questions honestly near the school. August meets Dev Okafor, editor of the school paper, who's investigating why three seniors transferred out mid-year with no forwarding address. Beat: intrigue.

chapters.title: What Dev Found
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He shows August a century of yearbooks: every graduating class lists a 'First Voice,' a student honored for an essay no one can find copies of. The First Voices' photos all show students who left town immediately after graduation — or whose entries end abruptly. Beat: dread disguised as journalistic excitement.

chapters.title: The Undercroft
chapters.summary: August's POV. Following vibrations in the floor during third period, August and Dev find a sealed stairwell behind the gym leading down to the old quarry face, where the essay prompt is carved into living stone. Her throwaway answer is already etched there, growing deeper each day. Beat: awe curdling into fear.

chapters.title: Honest Answers
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. They test it: Dev reads a true statement aloud in the undercroft and the stone drinks his words; afterward he can't remember saying them. August realizes the missing seniors answered too completely. The quarry doesn't take lives — it takes the part of you that meant them. Beat: horror of comprehension.

chapters.title: The Crane Name
chapters.summary: August's POV. In the town archive she finds the founding charter: Ezekiel Crane traded the quarry his descendants' honesty in exchange for the town's prosperity. Every generation, a Crane must serve as First Voice. Her mother didn't abandon her — she was taken by her own answer years ago. Beat: grief reframing everything.

chapters.title: Everyone Knows Something
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. The essay deadline approaches and classmates begin answering honestly — small confessions first, then devastating ones. The town glows brighter as students dim. August watches her best friend Priya give up her ambition to be a surgeon and feel nothing about losing it. Beat: moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Priya's Empty Page
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Once the quarry's most brilliant student, now hollowed and serene, Priya explains why surrendering your truth feels like peace. August realizes the quarry doesn't just feed — it convinces. Beat: temptation; August nearly envies her.

chapters.title: Mr. Voss's Confession
chapters.summary: August's POV. Voss reveals he was almost First Voice twenty years ago and stopped himself at the last word; he's been half-empty ever since, teaching only so he could warn someone. He gives her Ezekiel Crane's original journal. Beat: mentorship and guilt.

chapters.title: The Journal
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. The journal reveals the loophole Ezekiel hid from the town council: the covenant renews only if the First Voice answers freely and completely. A coerced or partial answer breaks it — but breaking it means the town loses everything the quarry provides, possibly including the ground itself. Beat: hope with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: Counting Days Again
chapters.summary: August's POV. Graduation is nine days away; the ceremony is the renewal rite. August drafts her real answer — what she'd die to protect — and feels the stone pulling at her already. She starts lying to everyone, even Dev, to keep her truth safe. Beat: isolation deepening.

chapters.title: The Lie That Worked
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Hurt by August's coldness, Dev investigates alone and discovers the council has known for generations — the mayor's office keeps the ledger of First Voices. He also learns the transferred seniors aren't gone; they're in a care facility downtown, alive and smiling and vacant. Beat: betrayal and resolve.

chapters.title: Council of Granite
chapters.summary: August's POV. Confronted, Mayor Ashford argues the covenant is mercy: one student's truth per generation versus a whole town's survival. Her own daughter was First Voice in 1998. 'You'd trade us for a feeling?' she asks. August has no clean answer. Beat: the antagonist becomes almost sympathetic.

chapters.title: What August Would Die For
chapters.summary: August's POV. Alone at the quarry rim, August finally admits her truth: not freedom, not escape — belonging. She wants, desperately, to belong somewhere, and the quarry has been offering that all along. The stone begins to accept her. Beat: the villain is her own loneliness.

chapters.title: Nine Voices
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The nine previous First Voices, sensing a renewal near, surface in August's dreams and show her their memories — including her mother's last full day, spent happy, choosing this. August wakes weeping and furious. Beat: despair at its lowest point.

chapters.title: Breaking Ground
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev and Priya — who remembers enough of her old self to fight — plan to collapse the undercroft before graduation. But demolition permits require the mayor, and the dynamite in the maintenance shed is real. The plan is set for the night of the ceremony. Beat: momentum and recklessness.

chapters.title: Graduation Eve
chapters.summary: August's POV. The town throws a festival so bright it's obscene. August says goodbye to her grandmother, who slips her Ezekiel's final letter: he regretted the bargain and built the loophole hoping a descendant would be brave enough to lose everything rather than feed. Beat: quiet courage gathering.

chapters.title: The Ceremony
chapters.summary: August's POV. On stage in cap and gown, microphone live, the whole town waiting for the First Voice's reading, August stands before the prompt. Dev's charges are set below; Priya holds the detonator. One word from her and either the covenant renews or the town falls. Beat: frozen moment at maximum tension.

chapters.title: An Honest Answer
chapters.summary: August's POV. August answers the prompt aloud — fully, freely — but her answer is refusal: 'Nothing. I won't die for this town. I'll live for it instead.' A free and complete answer that breaks the covenant's terms. The quarry screams; the ground shudders; the lights go out across Granite Falls. Beat: cathartic climax.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. The town survives — poorer, dimmer, real. The First Voices wake slowly; August's mother returns hollow but present, and August chooses to stay and help rebuild rather than flee. The quarry floods. Some townspeople hate her; some thank her; most just start over. Beat: bittersweet cost accounted.

chapters.title: The Next Prompt
chapters.summary: August's POV. Weeks later, August writes her actual college essay — the same prompt, answered honestly, for no stone to hear. She mails applications to schools far away and near, undecided for the first time, because staying might mean belonging too. Final line: she stops counting days. Beat: earned hope.
